definition_short: A king is in check when it is attacked by one or more enemy pieces.
definition_long:
FIDE Art. 3.9.1: 'The king is said to be in check if it is attacked by one or more of the opponent's pieces, even if such pieces are constrained from moving to the square occupied by the king because they would then leave or place their own king in check.'

The trailing clause matters and is routinely misunderstood: a PINNED piece still gives check. Art. 3.9.2: 'No piece can be moved that will either expose the king of the same colour to check or leave that king in check.' There is no rule requiring check to be announced, and no rule making it compulsory to escape by any particular means.

preconditions: A king stands on a square attacked by an enemy piece

exceptions: A pinned piece still delivers check — being unable to legally move does not stop a piece attacking the king.
limitations: Check is not a threat to be evaluated; it is a state. Being in check is not itself bad, and giving check is not itself good.

by_level.beginner: Your king is under attack. You must deal with it this move — move the king, block the line, or capture the attacker.
by_level.intermediate: Check. Only three replies exist: move the king, interpose, or capture the checking piece. Against a double check only the king move is available.
by_level.advanced: Art. 3.9.1. Note that a pinned piece still gives check.
